subject: surgery
title: Cervical Lymphadenopathy, Tuberculous Lymphadenitis, and Cold Abscess

steps.tx: Evaluation of **cervical lymphadenopathy** requires systematic examination of all cervical lymphatic stations. Clinicians divide neck nodes into six standardized levels: submental and submandibular nodes in level one, upper deep jugular nodes in level two, mid-jugular nodes in level three, lower jugular nodes in level four, posterior triangle nodes in level five, and pretracheal central compartment nodes in level six. Distinguishing reactive hyperplasia from infectious, granulomatous, or metastatic disease governs management.
steps.say: Cervical lymph nodes are organized into six anatomical levels from the submental space to the posterior triangle. Accurate level mapping guides identification of the underlying infection or malignancy.

rows: Level I (A & B)
Submental and submandibular triangles above hyoid bone
Lip, anterior floor of mouth, oral tongue tip, buccal mucosa
Level II (A & B)
Skull base down to hyoid bone, bounded by posterior SCM border
Oropharynx, larynx, oral cavity, hypopharynx, parotid gland
Level III (Mid Jugular)
Hyoid bone superiorly to cricoid cartilage inferiorly
Larynx, hypopharynx, oral tongue, thyroid gland lateral lobes
Level IV (Low Jugular)
Cricoid cartilage to clavicle; includes Virchow node on left
Thyroid gland, cervical esophagus, thoracic and abdominal viscera
Level V (Posterior)
Posterior triangle bounded by trapezius, SCM, and clavicle
Nasopharynx, posterior scalp, cutaneous neck, thyroid
Level VI (Central)
Hyoid to sternal notch between carotid sheaths
Thyroid gland, glottic and subglottic larynx, cervical trachea

steps.tx: In developing countries, Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection remains the most common etiology of persistent granulomatous neck masses, termed **tuberculous lymphadenitis** or scrofula. It accounts for thirty to forty percent of all extrapulmonary tuberculosis cases. The primary route of entry involves hematogenous seeding following pulmonary infection, or retrograde lymphatic spread from mycobacteria colonizing the tonsillar crypts. The posterior triangle and upper deep jugular lymph node chains are the most frequently affected sites.
steps.say: Tuberculous lymphadenitis, or scrofula, is the leading cause of chronic cervical adenopathy in endemic regions, typically involving posterior triangle and jugulodigastric nodes.

nodes.label: Central Caseation Necrosis in Lymph Nodes

steps.tx: The natural progression of untreated tuberculous lymphadenitis follows five distinct pathological and clinical stages. In stage one, affected lymph nodes are discrete, firm, and non-tender. As inflammation breaches the nodal capsule in stage two, periadenitis glues adjacent nodes into a fixed, conglomerate mass termed **matted tuberculous nodes**. Stage three features central caseous necrosis and liquefaction, transforming the matted nodal mass into a cold abscess that lacks warmth, erythema, and acute pain.
steps.say: Tuberculous adenitis progresses from discrete firm nodes to matted conglomerate masses. Central caseous liquefaction then creates a painless cold abscess devoid of acute inflammatory erythema.

rows: Stage 1 (Hyperplasia)
Reactive follicular and epithelioid cell hyperplasia
Discrete, mobile, firm, rubbery, painless lymphadenopathy
Stage 2 (Periadenitis)
Capsular breach with perilymphadenitis and adhesions
Matted, non-mobile conglomerate mass adherent to surrounding tissue
Stage 3 (Cold Abscess)
Central caseation liquefaction within node capsule
Fluctuant swelling devoid of warmth, redness, or acute tenderness
Stage 4 (Collar Stud)
Perforation through deep fascia into subcutaneous space
Dumbbell collection with palpable cross-fluctuance across fascia
Stage 5 (Sinus Tract)
Spontaneous cutaneous rupture and chronic drainage
Chronic ulcer or sinus with characteristic undermined, bluish edges

steps.tx: When a deep subfascial caseous lymph node undergoes liquefaction, accumulating fluid pressure causes central necrosis of the overlying investing layer of deep cervical fascia. The liquefied pus herniates through this narrow fascial aperture into the looser superficial subcutaneous tissue, forming a **collar stud abscess**. Known in classical surgical literature as an abscessus en bouton de chemise, this bilocular collection comprises a deep necrotic lymph node connected via a constricted fascial neck to an expansive subcutaneous reservoir.
steps.say: A collar stud abscess forms when caseous pus from a deep lymph node erodes through a small fascial opening into the subcutaneous plane, creating a classic hourglass collection.

left.title: Superficial Subcutaneous Compartment
points: Situated superficial to investing layer of deep cervical fascia
Expansile, soft, fluctuant subcutaneous fluid collection
Lacks overlying erythema, calor, or classical pyogenic signs
Readily compressible, transferring fluid into deeper compartment

right.title: Deep Subfascial Nodal Compartment
points: Originates from necrotic caseating deep cervical lymph node
Situated deep to investing fascia near jugular vein and SCM
Harbors the primary granulomatous nidus of mycobacterial disease
Communicates with superficial space through a tight fascial ring

steps.tx: The pathognomonic physical examination sign of a collar stud abscess is cross-fluctuance. Alternating digital pressure between the superficial subcutaneous reservoir and the deeper subfascial lymph node transmits a distinct fluid wave across the constricted fascial neck. An indispensable surgical rule governs its drainage: simple incision over the subcutaneous swelling is strictly contraindicated because **blind superficial incisional drainage** leaves the deep subfascial nidus unaddressed and results in an intractable, non-healing tuberculous sinus.
steps.say: Cross-fluctuance confirms the connection between deep and superficial pockets. Incising only the superficial bulge leaves the deep focus behind, leading to a persistent discharging sinus.

nodes.label: Fluid Wave Transmitted Across Fascial Neck
Error: Simple Incision of Superficial Pocket
Chronic Scrofuloderma Sinus Tract with Undermined Edges

steps.tx: If a collar stud abscess spontaneously ruptures through ischemic skin, or is incised improperly, it forms a tuberculous sinus, also known as scrofuloderma. The cutaneous ulcer exhibits thin, undermined, bluish-purple edges and a pale base covered by watery discharge and curdy caseous debris. Aspiration of cold abscesses must always be performed through **oblique needle aspiration** traversing healthy surrounding skin rather than dependent necrotic skin, ensuring an intact soft tissue seal that prevents sinus tract formation.
steps.say: Rupture of a cold abscess produces a chronic sinus with undermined bluish edges. Aspiration must always be directed obliquely through healthy skin to avoid creating a sinus.

rows: Oblique Healthy Skin Entry
Wide-bore needle inserted obliquely through normal distant skin
Creates stepped valvular tract that closes after withdrawal, preventing fistula
Direct Dependent Puncture
Perpendicular needle insertion directly over point of maximal skin thinning
Strictly contraindicated; inevitably breaks down into a chronic discharging sinus
Ultrasound-Guided Aspiration
Real-time transducer guidance directing cannula into deep pocket
Evacuates thick caseous necrotic material while mapping deep fascial defect

steps.tx: Definitive diagnosis of tuberculous lymphadenitis relies on fine-needle aspiration cytology, Ziehl-Neelsen staining for acid-fast bacilli, and real-time polymerase chain reaction testing, such as **cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification**. Cytology demonstrates caseating granulomas composed of epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans multinucleated giant cells, and granular acellular necrotic debris. Modern molecular testing simultaneously confirms Mycobacterium tuberculosis and detects rpoB gene mutations conferring rifampicin resistance within two hours.
steps.say: Fine-needle aspiration with GeneXpert PCR testing confirms tuberculous adenitis and detects rifampicin resistance within hours, identifying caseating granulomas and Langhans giant cells.

rows: FNAC Cytology
Epithelioid granulomas, Langhans giant cells, amorphous caseous necrosis
High sensitivity (85-90%); establishes granulomatous architecture
Ziehl-Neelsen (ZN) Staining
Bright red, slender, rod-shaped acid-fast bacilli on blue background
Variable sensitivity (30-50%); depends directly on nodal bacterial load
CBNAAT (GeneXpert)
Automated real-time PCR targeting Mycobacterium tuberculosis IS6110 sequence
Exceptional sensitivity (>90%) with rapid detection of rifampicin resistance
Mycobacterial Culture (MGIT)
Automated liquid culture detection of viable mycobacterial colonies
Gold standard for comprehensive second-line antibiotic sensitivity profiling

steps.tx: The cornerstone of management is medical treatment with standard six-month **anti-tubercular therapy**, consisting of a two-month intensive phase of rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by a four-month continuation phase of rifampicin and isoniazid. Surgical intervention is restricted strictly to diagnostic excisional biopsy of indeterminate nodes, aspiration of tense symptomatic cold abscesses, or en bloc excision of localized sinus tracts and underlying necrotic nodes that fail to resolve despite compliant chemotherapy.
steps.say: Treatment is medical, utilizing a six-month anti-tubercular chemotherapy regimen. Surgery is reserved for diagnostic biopsy or evacuating tense abscesses that fail medical therapy.

nodes.label: Surgical Excision Reserved for Persistent Cold Abscess
